title: Dancing Dodson puts the band on stage at the Regent Theater
summary: His first theater appearance goes badly until Dodson steps in, and the band wins over the audience.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: And so, I worked on that line. Well, when I left, I got a new experience, because along comes a man -- was it there? Wait a minute now. No, I'm ahead of my story. Let me tell you something that happened. There was a dancer when we was down at Baron's, named Yonder.

Y-o-n-d-e-r. Wait a minute, what was his name? I can't think of his name now. But, this dancer was as good as Bill Robinson. But he made one mistake. He went into -- he left for Waterville to go for the burlesque. And burlesque is a step below vaudeville.. See, instead of going up. So, anyhow, Dancing Dodson was his name. Dancing Dodson. Well, Dodson came to us and here was another experience that we had

that was very good, because he was working at the Regent Theater. And he heard about the band, so we had a nice little band there, so he come down one day to listen to the band and he was talking to Bricktop and a couple of other entertainers there. So he said, "How would you boys like to come on and try to -- have you ever been on stage?" We said "no we hadn't". So he said, "Well, I'll tell you what I'm going to do. I'm going to give you a chance. I'm going to bring you down there and let you do a couple of numbers in my show." He was a single. So he said, "Alright, polish up your horns and get your shoes shined and everything and get yourself together and come on down to the theater." Now the Regent Theater is 116th Street and 7th Avenue. And so, he put us on. He got out there and said -- okay, he introduced us, see, and we were ready to play. See, and the curtain come up -- and, well when we started off, we sounded like a bunch of cats yelling. Well, what happened, everybody was scared to death because all these guys, you know, we had come up from Atlantic City and we had never been into a theater. Elmon Chambers couldn't find his mouth. He couldn't find the embouchure. And the trombone player was just blowing. He didn't know. And to me, it looked just like two keys, one big white key and one big black key. That's all I could see. And I know we must have sounded like the devil. We really sounded like the devil.

And so, we sounded so terrible that Dodson came out on the stage and said, "Wait a minute, that's enough of this foolishness." He said, "Let me straighten you guys out. After all, you're here to play some good music for the people, not to clown and kid like you would in the cabaret." You know? But that settled us. We went on and did very fine for that show. And he kept us there for two or three days, you know. Because it wasn't paid. But that was our first chance.

Now, the second chance I got was an act. The first time I was ever on stage. But, I'm telling you, it was a horrible feeling. The sweat rolled down on us and, (laugh), (unintelligible). And I couldn't find nothing.
And then Elmer Chambers, he said, "I tried very hard, but I couldn't find my mouth." And you know, he couldn't get the horn on his chops.
And poor Horton was blowing everything out, you see?

So, anyhow, but after he did that -- he coming out and saying that, it changed the whole picture. Then we went into a little number like, "Toot, Toot, Tootsie, Good-bye", something like that. And the people liked it very much, you see. That was my first chance on the stage, see?
